sn11.12:1.3: _Maghavā_ (“bounteous one”) is a common epithet of Indra (eg. Rig Veda 3.39.09a, Atharva Veda 8.4.19a, Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 24.5.22). It is from the Vedic _magha_, “gift, bounty”. The name Māgha, with the same meaning, is a name of Sakka at [sn2.3](), while at [snp3.5:1.3]() a brahmin student Māgha asks about generosity. Finally, the good king of [mn83]() is named Maghadeva, “god of bounty”. The passage here attributes the name to his ancestry, but it goes on to praise his generosity.
sn11.12:2.1: _Purandara_ (“Fortbreaker”) is another epithet (eg. Rig Veda 1.102.7). The Buddha reforms it to _Purindada_ (“Firstgiver”) at [sn11.12:2.1](). But Indra’s generosity is long renowned: “He is the able one, and he will be able for us—Indra who distributes the goods” (Rig Veda 1.10.6).
sn11.12:3.1: _Sakka_ (_śakra_, the “able one”) was originally an epithet of Indra (as per previous note).
sn11.12:4.1: Vāsava means “endowed with wealth” (_vasu_; see for example Rig Veda 1.9.9a _indraṁ vasupatiṁ_ “Indra, lord of wealth”). This passage, rather, plays on the word _āvasatha_ and calls him the “giver of a guesthouse”. Later Brahmanical texts enumerated eight Vasus, with Indra as their lord, who are reckoned among the thirty-three.
sn11.12:5.1: “Thousand eyes” is _sahassakkha_, more commonly _sahassanetta_ [sn11.9:2.3](), [snp2.12:5.4](), [thag21.1:58.4]()). In the Rig Veda it describes the sparkle of the Soma, perhaps alluding to its visionary effects (9.60, 9.65.7). It is in this context that Indra, along with Vāyu, is first called “thousand-eyed” (1.23.3). It is also used for Agni, the fire with eyes all around (1.79.12, 10.79.5). | “Needs” (_atthā_) here recalls [sn11.8:5.1]().
sn11.12:6.1: Sanskrit sources know his wife as Śacī (“the powerful”), daughter of the titan maiden Pulomā, who came to be known as Indrāṇī. The Pali _sujampati_ (“Sujā’s husband”) evidently draws from Indra’s epithet _śacīpati_ (“lord of power”; Rig Veda 1.106.06, 4.30.17, 8.15.13). But as Śacī Paulomī she is also author of a Vedic hymn in her own right (10.159). There she gains power through the same oblation by which Indra gained his power. She does this in order to gain victory over her co-wives and husband (“only my will should my husband follow”; “I will rule widely over this hero and over his people”). Indra was evidently not threatened by such a powerful woman and took her to wife. _Sujā_ should be considered the Pali spelling of _śacī_. These indomitable characters forged a harmonious relationship, as seen when they share domestic duties by working together at the loom ([ud3.7:3.2]()).
sn11.12:7.1: The concept of 33 gods goes back as far as Rig Veda 8.28.1. The number is a reduplication of the trinity. In Buddhist texts they are not enumerated, but Yājñavalkya reckons them as eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, plus Indra and Prajāpati (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.2). The final pair are elsewhere said to be Dyaus (“Heaven” = Zeus) and Pṛthivī (“Earth”), or the twin Aśvins.
